author: BrentDesk Research
headline: DataVolt and KACST join the Saudi Mega Projects agenda in Riyadh
deck: DataVolt and KACST appear alongside the destination developers, because compute capacity has become an infrastructure programme.
excerpt: DataVolt and KACST appear on the Saudi Mega Projects agenda alongside the destination developers, reflecting how far data centre capacity has moved into the infrastructure conversation.
content:
Two names on the Saudi Mega Projects agenda in Riyadh do not belong to destination developers: Abdulaziz AlMubarak of DataVolt and Dr Bandar Alkahlan of KACST, the King Abdulaziz City for Science and Technology.

Their presence on a giga-project platform reflects a reclassification that has happened quickly. Data centre capacity used to be procured as commercial real estate with unusual services requirements. It is now planned as national infrastructure, on the same footing as power generation or ports, because the constraint on artificial intelligence capability has turned out to be physical rather than computational — land, power, cooling and connectivity, in that order.

Saudi Arabia's position on the first two is strong. Land is available at scale, and the generation build-out gives access to power at prices and volumes that most jurisdictions cannot match. The third is where the difficulty concentrates. Data centre cooling in a climate with high ambient temperatures for much of the year consumes energy in direct proportion to how hot it is outside, and the water-based cooling that is most efficient elsewhere is constrained in a country where fresh water is desalinated. The design compromises that follow are the technical substance of building this capacity in the Gulf.

This publication has covered the industrial supply chain forming behind it, including Alfanar's $150m commitment to data centre components with an HPE server line reaching 700 units a month, and Mawani's lease of Ras Al-Khair port land to China's ZTT for a SAR 375m subsea cable plant. Those are the manufacturing and connectivity halves of the same programme.

KACST's presence points at the research and standards dimension. A national compute programme raises questions about sovereign control of data, about what workloads run domestically, and about the local capability to design and operate at this scale rather than importing it wholesale — the same institutional capability question that arises in rail systems integration.

The connection to the destination projects is more direct than it appears. The giga-projects are being designed as instrumented environments, with building management, mobility, utility and security systems generating and consuming data continuously. Where that processing happens, who operates it and what it costs are infrastructure decisions taken at master-planning stage, not IT decisions taken later.

This publication has also noted that the hardest part of Saudi Arabia's technology build begins after handover, when these systems have to be operated and maintained rather than installed.

Speaker names come from the organiser's published agenda. The power question is the one that will decide siting, and it is being answered now rather than at commissioning.
